strengths: Novel hierarchical identity-preserving attention mechanism (intra-subject, inter-subject, cross-modal) that is well-motivated as an alternative to naive token concatenation used by prior work such as Phantom and Concat-ID.
Integration of a pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as a semantically richer conditioning encoder than standard text encoders, with an ablation confirming its contribution to text-video alignment.

First application (to the authors' knowledge) of online RL (Flow-GRPO with a composite quality/identity reward) to the multi-subject subject-consistent video generation setting, addressing known limitations of standard diffusion losses in aligning fine-grained identity concepts.

Extensive quantitative comparison against many open-source (Phantom, SkyReels-A2, VACE) and proprietary (Vidu, Pika, Kling) baselines, with consistent improvements across FaceSim, GmeScore, NexusScore, and NaturalScore.
Thorough ablation studies (hierarchical attention, VLM encoder, curated data) with both quantitative (Table 2) and qualitative (Figure 5) evidence isolating each component's contribution.

A new large-scale, carefully curated multi-source dataset (OpenS2V-Nexus-based, synthetic, and professionally shot video) with documented statistics and a comparison of reference-image construction strategies (data augmentation vs. Flux-Kontext vs. GPT-4o vs. their Gemini-based pipeline), which could be a useful community resource if released as promised.
Demonstrated downstream applicability to zero-shot controllable video editing (subject replacement, background modification), broadening potential impact beyond the core generation task.
weaknesses: Section B.2 'Details of Reward Calculation,' which should specify how R_qual and R_id are computed and how reward hacking is mitigated (a claim made in the related work), is essentially empty in the manuscript as provided, leaving a core novel component (the RL reward design) underspecified and hindering reproducibility.
No quantitative ablation isolates the online RL stage's contribution; only qualitative examples (Figure 5, right panel) are shown, while Table 2 ablates only architecture and data, not RL vs. no-RL.

Evaluation relies entirely on automated/learned metrics (FaceSim, GmeScore, NexusScore, NaturalScore) computed with the authors' own or other model-based scorers; no human/user study is reported to validate perceptual quality, identity preservation, or prompt alignment claims, despite such claims being central to the paper.

Evaluation set size (180 unique subject-text pairs from a single benchmark, OpenS2V-Nexus) is relatively narrow for establishing generalization across the wide range of scenarios (objects, environments, nature) the dataset claims to cover; no variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported.

No analysis of computational cost, inference latency, or parameter count trade-offs relative to baselines, despite the model integrating a 7B VLM plus a 14B DiT backbone—an important practical consideration acknowledged only briefly as a limitation without supporting numbers.

The data curation pipeline depends on proprietary tools (Gemini-Flash-Image, Qwen2.5-VL, Grounding DINO, SAM) for subject decomposition and captioning; while code/data release is promised, reliance on closed-source generative components for the training data itself raises reproducibility and long-term availability concerns.
Minor inconsistencies in metric naming between Table 1 ('GmeScore') and Table 2 ('Text-Video Align.') could confuse readers about whether these are the same metric.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated hierarchical identity-preserving attention (intra-subject, inter-subject, cross-modal) that is ablated stage-by-stage, showing consistent, interpretable gains in FaceSim/NexusScore.

First application (to the authors' knowledge) of online RL (GRPO/Flow-GRPO) with a composite, task-specific reward (fidelity + quality, including a NaturalScore term to counter reward hacking) to multi-subject video diffusion; ablations on reward components and comparison to offline DPO support the design choices.

Integrates a pretrained VLM (Qwen2.5-VL) as a semantic/cross-modal grounding module rather than a conventional text encoder, with an ablation showing measurable alignment gains over a single T5 encoder.

Constructs and will release a large-scale curated multi-subject video dataset via a non-trivial VLM + image-editing pipeline, with reasonable statistics and comparison against alternative reference-construction strategies (data augmentation, Flux-Kontext, GPT-4o).

Reasonably broad empirical validation: quantitative comparison to multiple open-source and proprietary baselines, qualitative comparisons, an ablation table, and a human preference study (200 questionnaires, 30 participants) that corroborates automated metrics and partially addresses circularity/reward-hacking concerns.
Demonstrates a useful downstream application (zero-shot subject-consistent video editing) beyond the core generation task.
weaknesses: Several evaluation metrics used for both training reward and testing (NexusScore, NaturalScore) are derived from the authors' own benchmark/pipeline, raising concern about circularity/self-serving evaluation despite the human study; the human study itself only compares against 4 baselines with a modest participant pool.

The 14B 'large-scale' model underperforms the smaller 1.3B RL-tuned model on several key metrics (e.g., FaceSim 60.71% vs 66.10%) in Table 1, and this counter-intuitive scaling result is not explained or discussed in the text.
A broken cross-reference ('Tab. ??') in Section 4.3 indicates incomplete proofreading/compilation, a minor but non-trivial presentation flaw.

The ethics statement claims the dataset avoids real-world public figures, yet Figures 1 and 4 explicitly show generation with recognizable public figures (e.g., Albert Einstein, apparent Taylor Swift reference in Fig. 2's example prompt), which is inconsistent with the stated mitigation and raises a minor ethical/representational concern.

The core technical contribution is largely a careful integration of existing techniques (Flow-GRPO/GRPO, VLM encoders, hierarchical cross-attention, DreamBooth-style curation) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; novelty is more in combination/application than in algorithmic invention.

Evaluation set size (180 subject-text pairs) is relatively small for claims of general robustness across 'complex, real-world scenarios', and there is no analysis of failure cases, limits on number of subjects, or robustness beyond the examples shown.

Code/model/dataset release is stated as future ('will be released'), so reproducibility cannot be independently verified from the manuscript alone; several hyperparameters (e.g., reward weight choices) appear empirically set without deeper justification of sensitivity beyond one ablation table.
